NISAR velocity requirement validation

Each requirement is evaluated against GPS three ways (speed, vx, vy) using mosaic3d -obsDump rows at the GPS pixels, with the GPS forward-modelled through the solver's own weights and windows. Status is green when the RMS residual over stations is within the 1-σ tolerance now, amber when the fitted error curve reaches it at 30 cycles, red otherwise, grey when the data cannot test it.

Fraction = RMS over points of (speed error / that point's tolerance 0.03·V + c), the per-point statistic the status is judged on; it is not achieved ÷ tolerance, which divides pooled averages and differs when the tolerance varies across points.

Validation data sources

Greenland GPS stations (NIL1, NIL2, NIL3, NIL4, NIL5, NIU1, NIU2, NIU3, NIU4, NIU5). Continuous GNSS stations deployed for NISAR cal/val (May 2024 to Aug 2026). Positions come from the NISAR cal/val database: 30 s solutions through the sunlit season and a single daily session in winter (Antarctic winter solutions are flagged degraded and excluded). Velocities are least-squares slopes of position over each observation's own window; antenna resets are detected as off-flow position steps and removed. Slow (< 50 m/yr) and fast classes are set by the long-term GPS speed.

Antarctica GPS stations (NIT0, NIT1, NIT2, NIT3, NIT4, NIT7). Continuous GNSS stations deployed for NISAR cal/val (Jan 2024 to Mar 2026). Positions come from the NISAR cal/val database: 30 s solutions through the sunlit season and a single daily session in winter (Antarctic winter solutions are flagged degraded and excluded). Velocities are least-squares slopes of position over each observation's own window; antenna resets are detected as off-flow position steps and removed. Slow (< 50 m/yr) and fast classes are set by the long-term GPS speed.

2000 m points (45 of 152). In-situ GPS velocities measured along the 2000 m elevation contour of the Greenland ice sheet in 1993 to 1997 (NSIDC-0615, NSIDC-0615). Because these are single epochs roughly a quarter century old, each point was screened for change since it was measured: the Sentinel-1 annual velocity stack (2014-15 to 2022-23) gives a linear trend at every point, and only points south of 77 N whose trend projected over the gap is less than half the requirement tolerance (0.03·V + 1 or + 5 m/yr) are kept. The screen is on trend, not year-to-year scatter, which is nearly independent of it. The retained 45 span 1 to 150 m/yr (24 slow, 21 fast); only two are below 6 m/yr, so the set does not test the slowest ice. Each point is a single velocity, so its reference is constant in time.

NEGIS points (63). GPS velocities of the 63-pole strain net around the EastGRIP drill site on the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream, observed 2015 to 2019 (Hvidberg, C. S. et al. (2020). Surface velocity of the Northeast Greenland Ice Stream (NEGIS): assessment of interior velocities derived from satellite data by GPS. The Cryosphere 14, 3487-3502. doi:10.5194/tc-14-3487-2020). The poles span 10 to 58 m/yr (52 slow, 11 fast) across the stream and its shear margin. No point was culled: the GPS epoch falls inside the Sentinel-1 annual stack (2014-15 to 2022-23), whose mean reads 1.001 of the GPS speed (median over the 63), so the ice has not measurably changed. Each point is a single velocity, so its reference is constant in time.

Summit points (9). Nine GNSS stations within about 35 km of Summit, Greenland, at 0.5 to 2.3 m/yr, from annual solutions for 2022, 2023 and 2024 averaged (Pickell, D. & Hawley, R. (2024). An East-West Network of Twelve Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) Stations in the Summit Region of Greenland: RINEX Data, 2022-2025. Arctic Data Center. doi:10.18739/A2183446Q). Because the speeds are comparable to the 1 m/yr floor of the slow requirement they bound an additive error rather than a scale, and because they share frames the effective sample size is nearer one than nine. Each is a single velocity, constant in time.
